transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-15 16:00 PT; Duration: 64m; Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Singh (AeroFlux SRE), Marta Ortega (AeroFlux ML Platform), Samir Nadeem (AeroFlux CTO)

Summary: (auto) We went through SLO options for latency and throughput; settled on a measurement playbook that mixes synthetic runner tests with sampled production traffic; action items and timelines agreed.

[00:00] Lena (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[00:10] Ravi: Ravi here, SRE. Marta and Samir are here as well.
[00:15] Marta: hi, thanks.
[00:18] Marcus (SE): Marcus from Redwood. Quick agenda: TTFT vs TPOT definitions, target percentiles, sampling plan and bench cadence, then next steps.
[00:28] Samir: sounds good. I think the main thing for us is predictable p95 under our normal load and graceful behavior under spikes, since AeroFlux can't have chat timeouts during peak telemetry ingestion windows.
[00:39] Lena: exactly. maybe start with definitions so we align: when we say TTFT we mean time-to-first-token measured from request arrival to the first byte outgoing; TPOT is time-per-output-token or per-token latency after first token — often reported as per-token tail latency or per-response average.
[00:54] Ravi: we sometimes see long tails in the right tail; p99s spike during heavy concurrency. Curious how Redwood measures — are you measuring at the proxy or inside the runtime?
[01:05] Marcus: good q; our production bench measures at the ingress edge (RTT+queueing) and also exposes the runtime-internal metrics (scheduling wait, KV-cache miss cost). For the POC we propose both: edge-level TTL (sic) — sorry edge-level TTFT/TPOT measurement — plus a runtime slice so we can diagnose where tail comes from.
[01:25] Marta: do you have a recommended baseline target?
[01:28] Lena: Based on similar customers, for a chat-style prompt mix with median prompt length ~90 tokens, we usually aim for TTFT p95 < 180ms and TPOT p95 ~ 30–45ms for mainstream large models. For p99 we'd expect TTFT < 500ms and TPOT p99 < 120–150ms. But those numbers change with model size and quantization.
[01:47] Samir: hmm those are helpful. AeroFlux target is tighter — we want p95 TTFT <= 150ms if possible, because our UI shows first reply latency to customers. Are those achievable on Redwood hosted for a model close to 13B?
[02:02] Marcus: 13B unquantized on A100 class-ish will approach that for 1-2 token first responses depending on burstiness. Our recommendation: use prefix caching and KV-cache warm runs. Also consider a smaller distilled variant for first-token fallbacks to guarantee lower TTFT for tail cases.
[02:20] Ravi: fallback model — you mean route to a smaller checkpoint when queue depth > X? we worry about quality regressions in fallbacks.
[02:28] Lena: yes, the POC plan includes quality regression checks: we compare a sample of responses from fallback vs primary across BLEU-like similarity or a small eval set. If similarity below threshold, we don't route. It's an explicit policy.
[02:40] Marta: ok, how do you want our traffic sample? we can provide 7-day histograms, per-hour qps, and a set of 1k prompts anonymized.
[02:50] Marcus: perfect — we ask for the histogram, a stratified sample by prompt length buckets (0–50, 51–200, 201–1000). We'll synthesize the same distribution in the load generator and also do a production-sampled pass to validate.
[03:03] Samir: what's the bench cadence you recommend? simple steady-state, then spikes?
[03:09] Marcus: three-pass approach: 1) cold-start pass (clean cache) 30m with low concurrency to measure cold TTFT; 2) steady-state 30–60m warm-cache pass at your target qps to capture p95/p99; 3) spike & recovery: 10–15m ramp to 3–5× qps then observe tail and routing behavior. Repeat each scenario 3 times for statistical stability.
[03:34] Ravi: that makes sense. question on metrics — do you report at per-request level and can we get raw histograms?
[03:40] Marcus: yes, we provide per-request csv and pre-aggregated histograms for p50/p95/p99 and counts; plus token-level timing breakdown (e.g. scheduling wait, kernel exec, kv-cache miss penalty).
[03:50] Lena: we'll also provide a runbook to map our runtime metrics to your SLOs — e.g. how to interpret backend queueing vs network jitter.
[03:59] Marta: what about sampling rate? we can't stream all traffic to you for privacy.
[04:03] Marcus: we recommend stratified sampling at ~1–2% of requests for detailed payload capture, plus aggregated histograms at 100% (counts only). For POC we can do a higher sampling window (maybe 5%) for 48 hours to get a good dataset, with anonymization.
[04:17] Samir: on security, Marta will share constraints. do you need an on-prem pilot or is hosted ok?
[04:23] Lena: initial bench & measurement can be done on hosted/private redwood sandbox — if your compliance needs VPC we can plan a private pilot. For the measurement plan the metrics are the same; network and egress policies change the acceptance gating.
[04:36] Ravi: our acceptance criteria: during steady-state at target qps, p95 TTFT <= 150ms and p95 TPOT <= 40ms. If we fail these, we'll accept if there is an automated fallback to smaller model that keeps perceived latency under threshold and similarity to primary above 0.85 (we'll define metric).
[04:55] Marcus: ok let's capture that as the provisional acceptance. note that p99 targets will be more relaxed, but we'll track them for risk — p99 TTFT < 500ms and p99 TPOT < 150ms as an initial guardrail.
[05:08] Marta: how are you measuring tokenization differences? we use a proprietary tokeniser that differs from some open checkpoints.
[05:14] Marcus: we can instrument tokenization timing and normalize by token counts; for model-compat we recommend providing a tokenization mapping script or we run tokenization with your tokenizer in the harness.
[05:24] Lena: mapping out measurement instrumentation: 1) ingest edge timestamps (request received) 2) ingress to runtime handoff (queue) 3) kernel exec start/first-token-out 4) token emit times. We will correlate with ingest proxies so numbers reflect client-perceived latency.
[05:40] Ravi: do you surface confidence scores or hallucination checks as part of the quality regression?
[05:45] Marcus: not by default in the latency bench; for QA we run an eval set with similarity metrics and a small heuristic for hallucination detection — the bench artifacts will include those outputs so you can review.
[05:56] Samir: timeline — when can we run first pass?
[06:00] Lena: if you can share histograms and prompts by Monday (2026-09-20), Marcus can run initial synth passes the week of 9/21 and share results by 9/24. Then we sync to finalize pilot start end of that week.
[06:12] Marta: I'll confirm we can anonymize prompts; security will need to review the sandbox though.
[06:17] Ravi: what about flaky network noise — can you factor that out?
[06:20] Marcus: yes we tag runs with environment metadata and can run both in-region and cross-region to quantify network contribution; for the SLO we typically use in-region numbers unless your product has global calls.
[06:33] Lena: final bit on fallback policy: we'll prototype a routing policy that triggers at queue depth > X or observed TTFT p95 in rolling window > threshold; routing is per-request and has throttled capacity to avoid flapping. We'll document quality gating and a rollback plan.
[06:51] Samir: that addresses our primary concerns. any blockers?
[06:54] Marta: just security signoff and we need to see the initial numbers.
[06:58] Lena: great. we'll send the harness and the sample load JSON, plus a short README for the runs. Any other questions?
[07:05] Ravi: one small ask — include an example of CSV output and a sample plot of p95 vs concurrency so we can show stakeholders.
[07:11] Marcus: done, will include.
[07:14] Lena: thanks all. Recap in chat and action items.

(End meeting)
